DNS-over-HTTPS will eventually roll out in all major browsers, despite ISP opposition

As if enough things weren't already conspiratorial enough, I sense a false dichotomy here. We are being presented --

  • Option 1: DNS resolved by the OS as usual.
  • Option 2: HTTPS DNS resolved by the browser.

The missing option 3 is HTTPS DNS resolved by the OS. This looks like an attempt to smuggle in browser DNS under the banner of privacy, the result of which is a browser take-over of DNS operation away from the OS.

This would bypass both the /etc/hosts file and any protocol-based firewall rules, it would give browsers the privilege of censoring domains via an update, and it also raises a certificate trust problem which I'll describe in more detail below. The only benefit-of-doubt I can imagine is browsers implementing it as a crutch to help protect users with an OS which refuses to implement it.

To be sure, the ISPs definitely have no business collecting DNS resolve data, it's just that it isn't better to put things into the hands of browsers from companies diagnosed as SJW-positive.

The certificate problem is that any TLS connection, including HTTPS (that being HTTP over TLS), already uses/needs a resolved domain as part of its certificate check, which is a catch-22. To expand on that a bit:

  • The OS has a list of certificate authorities (CAs) which it trusts, meaning that TLS certs signed by one of those CAs are trusted.
  • Said CAs only sign certs for domains, not IP address.
  • Therefore, the process making a TLS connection needs to be using the domain as the host, not the IP address, otherwise the cert won't match.
  • That domain needs to be resolved before packets can start moving -- but this process is itself the resolver, which is an impasse.

The only correct solution I can see is if, just as with trusted CAs, it were possible to manage a list of trusted DNSs. Actually this is a perfect job for /etc/hosts, since pre-resolved DNSs can be added to that in advance, the authenticity of which then falls back to the CAs along with all other TLS connections.
